title: Greedy Best-First Finds the Route in Žižkov!
description: Watch Greedy Best-First sprint toward the goal by always expanding the node that looks closest, according to a heuristic. On a real street-map graph, it’s fast to visualize—but may trade optimality for speed.
ig_caption:
⚡️🗺️ Žižkov streets → one goal → Greedy Best-First!

In this visualization, **Greedy Best-First** is a graph search strategy that prioritizes the next intersection using only the **heuristic estimate** (typically distance-to-goal like straight-line / Euclidean). ✅

📌 **How it works (techy but real):**
- We model the street network as a **graph**: intersections = nodes, road segments = edges (often weighted by distance).
- The algorithm selects the open node with the **smallest h(n)** and expands it next.
- That means it *looks smart* locally: great for speed, but it can **get trapped in misleading shortcuts** because it doesn’t balance “cost so far” (no full g(n) like A*).

🔍 **On real maps:** With irregular blocks and connectivity changes in Žižkov, the heuristic guides exploration like a GPS guess—sometimes taking a scenic turn, sometimes reaching quickly.

👉 Want me to compare it vs. A* and Dijkstra on the same map? Comment your pick + share this reel to challenge a friend! 🚀
fb_caption:
Žižkov, Prague turned into a graph—nodes are intersections, edges are roads. 📍

This run uses **Greedy Best-First**: it always expands the next node with the smallest heuristic distance to the goal, so it can be extremely fast to find *a* path. 🤖

Want to see how it compares to Dijkstra or A* on the same street network? Share this post and drop a “VS” in the comments!

Keywords: Greedy Best-First, pathfinding algorithm, graph search, heuristic search, A* vs Greedy, Dijkstra comparison, real map visualization, computer science, coding tutorial.
